patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent visual symptoms and headache since age 18 — no current treatment
patient.hpi:
A 26-year-old Lebanese-American woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of recurrent episodes of visual disturbance followed by headache that she has experienced since age 18. She describes bright shimmering lines appearing in her peripheral vision (either side, unpredictable) that slowly grow into a large arc of flickering light, moving and expanding over approximately 25 minutes before disappearing. She sometimes sees a blind spot in the area where the lights were. After the visual phenomenon resolves, she develops a moderate-severe throbbing headache (6-8/10) with nausea and light sensitivity, lasting 4-8 hours.

Episodes occur 1-2 times per month and are triggered by stress, skipping meals, and the days before her period. She has used over-the-counter NSAIDs with partial relief. She has never consulted a neurologist or tried triptans. She initially attributed the visual symptoms to eye problems and had an ophthalmologic evaluation 3 years ago which was entirely normal (refraction, tonometry, fundoscopy all normal). The ophthalmologist suggested she see neurology but she did not follow up until now.

She is a graduate student, non-smoker, no alcohol. She has no medical history, takes no medications, and is not on contraception. She denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any headache that woke her from sleep.

family_history: Mother had migraines; no family history of glaucoma, stroke, or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Graduate student (chemistry); non-smoker; no alcohol; no illicit drugs; active lifestyle

physical_exam.neurological: Normal cranial nerves. Visual fields full by confrontation. PERRLA. No papilledema. Normal fundoscopy confirmed. Motor 5/5. DTR 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. Coordination and gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with typical visual aura (G43.1); untreated, triptan-naive

differential.key_features: Normal ophthalmologic evaluation (fundoscopy, tonometry, refraction) 3 years ago; episodic expanding visual aura is cortical in origin, not ocular
differential.distinguishing_test: Prior normal ophthalmology exam; brain MRI (normal)

differential.key_features: Visual seizures are brief (<2 min); expanding over 25 minutes is characteristic of cortical spreading depression; normal EEG; family history of migraine

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI to confirm no structural cause
Laboratory workup including ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies
Prescribe sumatriptan 100 mg for acute attacks
Counsel on trigger management and headache diary

critical_actions: Brain MRI for first neurology evaluation of visual aura
Prescribe triptan — patient has been undertreated for 8 years
Counsel on taking triptan at headache onset (not during aura)
Counsel on avoiding combined OCP in the future
contraindicated_actions: Do not take triptan during visual aura phase
Do not prescribe combined OCP in the future (migraine with aura)
Do not overuse analgesics (>15 days/month = MOH risk)
key_reasoning_points: Classic visual aura since age 18, family history, normal ophthalmologic evaluation — ICHD-3 criteria clearly met
Patient was undertreated for 8 years; initial referral by ophthalmologist was appropriate but not followed up
Normal brain MRI confirms primary migraine
Key action: initiate appropriate triptan treatment for 8 years of undertreatment

red_herrings.finding: Episodic monocular visual symptoms raising glaucoma concern
red_herrings.why_misleading: Recurrent visual disturbances in a young woman could suggest ocular disease (glaucoma, optic neuritis)
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior normal ophthalmologic evaluation; expanding visual aura is a cortical phenomenon (cortical spreading depression), not ocular; brain MRI normal

output.report:
TREATMENT FOR TRIPTAN-NAIVE MIGRAINE WITH AURA

RESULTS:
  ACUTE: Sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO at headache onset is first-line; 80% of patients respond. Can also use naratriptan (slower onset, fewer side effects) or eletriptan.
  COUNSELING: Take at headache onset NOT during visual aura. Naratriptan has longer half-life, useful for long attacks.
  PREVENTIVE: 1-2 attacks/month is borderline for preventive therapy; assess disability (MIDAS score). Topiramate, propranolol, or amitriptyline are options.

CONCLUSION: Start sumatriptan 100 mg; assess response in 3 months. Preventive therapy may not be needed if sumatriptan controls attacks adequately.
output.summary: Sumatriptan 100 mg first-line; take at headache onset; preventive therapy borderline given 1-2/month frequency

output.report:
SUMATRIPTAN PRESCRIPTION REVIEW

No contraindications. Normal BP. Not on OCPs. No cardiac disease. Prescribe sumatriptan 100 mg PO. Take at headache onset (not during aura). May repeat once after 2 hours (max 200 mg/day, max 9 days/month).

CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 100 mg safe and appropriate.
output.summary: Sumatriptan 100 mg safe; no contraindications; take at headache onset

output.report:
MIGRAINE TRIGGER MANAGEMENT EVIDENCE

KEY TRIGGERS AND STRATEGIES:
1. MEAL SKIPPING: Maintain regular meals with balanced protein; avoid fasting >4-5 hours
2. SLEEP: Maintain regular sleep schedule (same wake time weekends as weekdays); both too little AND too much sleep can trigger
3. STRESS: Biofeedback has Level A evidence for migraine prevention; mindfulness meditation Level B
4. HORMONAL: Menstrual-related migraines: peri-menstrual NSAIDs or mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan/naratriptan
5. HEADACHE DIARY: Essential to identify personal triggers; mobile apps (Migraine Buddy, Migraine Monitor) are validated tools

CONCLUSION: Headache diary, regular meals and sleep, stress management are adjunct non-pharmacological measures with good evidence.
output.summary: Regular meals, sleep schedule, and stress management; peri-menstrual mini-prophylaxis for predictable menstrual attacks; headache diary

output.impression: Normal EEG; no occipital epileptiform activity. Clinical correlation recommended.
